text:
Recent work supports selective history suppression, though this search found no exact 2024–2026 match combining NextItNet, context gates and controlled prefix interventions. [MSDCCL (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13878) combines soft weighting and hard denoising: weighting alone can retain noise, while deletion can discard useful interactions. [DyS4Rec (2025)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0893608025000139) learns personalized skips over irrelevant interactions using an LSTM; its transferable idea is interaction-level suppression, rather than choosing among whole block outputs.

Interest drift needs distinction from noise. [CoDeR (2025)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/33379) models demand shifts and applies counterfactual reasoning with backdoor adjustment; [CoDeR+ (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3778863) additionally treats user interest as a confounder. These motivate drift-sensitive forgetting, but do not establish that arbitrary prefix deletion identifies causal relevance. CoDeR+ also uses category-level interest information unavailable in this task.

Research hypothesis for the constrained experiment: retain one NextItNet backbone and scoring head; jointly learn sigmoid gates on historical convolution inputs, conditioned only on the causal context available at each position. Compare the same network on intact histories, removed older prefixes and matched random removals while preserving the recent suffix. Measure held-out next-item loss changes to distinguish harmless forgetting from lost predictive signal; use any consistency penalty cautiously because older context can be useful. This is a proposed adaptation, not a verified result from the cited papers. Preserve left padding and read the final nonpadding position; select using the fixed macro validation HR@10.
